name: Jim Lahey's No Knead Pizza Dough
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt introduces Jim Lahey's pizza dough from the book My Pizza as the pizza counterpart to the no-knead bread method Lahey and Mark Bittman popularized in 2006. The point of the long room-temperature rise, he explains, is that enzymes gradually chop the flour's large proteins into shorter pieces that link up into stretchy gluten sheets on their own, so you get the structure of a well-kneaded dough without kneading and without the oxidation kneading causes. Lahey himself adds a note saying the flour matters less than the handling: either bread or all-purpose is fine, but the dough should be stretched gently so it keeps its blistered, gassy character, and the balls should only be shaped just before topping. He offers two shaping approaches, one flat on the counter and a faster one rotating the disk on your knuckles.
comment_digest: Hydration is the recurring complaint, and cooks disagree on which direction it is wrong. One repeatedly added extra water to get a workable dough and also found it tore easily when stretching; another called it 'pizza soup,' too salty and too wet, needing a lot of added flour after it tripled at room temperature in 12 hours. Others accept the stickiness as normal, noting it barely matters since you hardly handle the dough. The 1 gram of yeast is widely questioned; one cook using active dry rather than instant used a heaping quarter teaspoon, and one who accidentally used quick-rise found the dough more than doubled in 6 hours, portioned it then and refrigerated it 12 hours with good results. Readers also note the video says 8 to 9 hours of rise against the recipe's 18, and that the video assumes shaped balls resting a couple of hours under a damp cloth, a step missing from the written recipe.
flags: 'Load More reviews' present, so only part of the 64 reviews is in the paste; a 'Featured Tweaks' block also appears above the review list and its entries are included. Several comments end with 'Read More' and may be truncated. Readers dispute the recipe's 1 g yeast and the rise time versus the linked video.
